arml-2025-power-01b.title: Systematic search

arml-2025-power-02a.title: Check small cases
arml-2025-power-02a.body:
Triples of distinct $\{2,3\}$-integers summing to $n$:
- $n=6$: $(1,2,3)$; $n=7$: $(1,2,4)$; $n=8$: $(1,3,4)$; $n=9$: $(1,2,6),(2,3,4)$; $n=10$: $(1,3,6)$; ($n\le5$: none, since the least sum of three parts is $1+2+3=6$).
- $n=11$: $(1,2,8)=1+2+2^3$, $(1,4,6)$, $(2,3,6)$: three representations.

No smaller $n$ has three, so the answer is $11$.

**Answer: 11**

arml-2025-power-02b.title: Odd number: one part is a power of 3
arml-2025-power-02b.body:
Since $2025$ is odd, exactly one of the two parts is odd, i.e. a power of $3$; call it $3^j$. Then $2025-3^j$ must be a $\{2,3\}$-integer, and $3^j\le2025<3^7=2187$ gives $j\le6$:
$$2025-1=2024=2^3\cdot11\cdot23,\ 2025-3=2022=2\cdot3\cdot337,\ 2025-9=2016=2^5\cdot3^2\cdot7,\ 2025-27=1998=2\cdot3^3\cdot37,$$
$$2025-81=1944=2^3\cdot3^5,\ 2025-243=1782=2\cdot3^4\cdot11,\ 2025-729=1296=2^4\cdot3^4.$$
Only $1944$ and $1296$ are $\{2,3\}$-integers. The representations are $(81,1944)$ and $(729,1296)$. (Exactly one part is odd: two odd parts, or two even parts, would give an even sum.)

**Answer: 2**

arml-2025-power-03.title: Ternary expansion
arml-2025-power-03.body: Let $3^s\le n<3^{s+1}$, so $s=\lfloor\log_3n\rfloor$, and write $n=\sum_{i=0}^sa_i3^i$ with $a_i\in\{0,1,2\}$. Each nonzero term $a_i3^i$ is $3^i$ or $2\cdot3^i$, a $\{2,3\}$-integer. These terms are pairwise distinct (different $i$ give different powers of $3$ in the odd part), so after sorting them we get a double-base representation of $n$ with at most $s+1=\lfloor\log_3n\rfloor+1$ parts. ∎

arml-2025-power-04a.title: Merge equal parts
arml-2025-power-04a.body: If the $n_k$ are distinct, sort them to obtain a double-base representation of length $r$. Otherwise two of them are equal, $n_i=n_j=a$; since $2a$ is again a $\{2,3\}$-integer, replacing the pair by the single part $2a$ writes $n$ as a sum of $r-1$ $\{2,3\}$-integers. Repeat. The number of terms strictly decreases each time, so the process stops (at the latest after $r-1$ steps), at which point all terms are distinct and, once sorted, form a double-base representation of length at most $r$. ∎

arml-2025-power-04b.title: Expand the square
arml-2025-power-04b.body:
Let $(n_1,\dots,n_\ell)$ be a double-base representation of $n$. Then
$$n^2=\sum_{i=1}^\ell n_i^2+\sum_{1\le i<j\le\ell}2n_in_j.$$
Each $n_i^2$ and each $2n_in_j$ is a $\{2,3\}$-integer (products and multiples by $2$ of $\{2,3\}$-integers are $\{2,3\}$-integers). The number of terms is $\ell+\binom\ell2=\binom{\ell+1}2$. By part (a), $n^2$ has a double-base representation with length at most $\binom{\ell+1}2$. ∎

arml-2025-power-05.title: Split one term
arml-2025-power-05.body:
Let $(n_1,\dots,n_r)$ be a signed double-base representation of $n\ne0$, so $r\ge1$, and write $|n_k|=2^{x_k}3^{y_k}$. Choose an index $i$ with $x_i+y_i$ maximal and replace $n_i$ by the two terms $3n_i$ and $-2n_i$. The sum is unchanged: $3n_i-2n_i=n_i$.

Both new terms have absolute value a $\{2,3\}$-integer ($3|n_i|=2^{x_i}3^{y_i+1}$ and $2|n_i|=2^{x_i+1}3^{y_i}$), and both have exponent sum $x_i+y_i+1$, which exceeds that of every other term, so neither coincides in absolute value with any remaining $n_k$ (in particular they differ from all remaining terms), and they differ from each other because $3n_i$ and $-2n_i$ have opposite signs ($n_i\ne0$). So after sorting we have $r+1$ distinct terms, a signed double-base representation of $n$ with length $r+1$. ∎

arml-2025-power-06a.title: Peel off one part at a time
arml-2025-power-06a.body:
**Key fact.** In a strictly-chained representation each part divides every later part, hence divides the sum of all parts from that part on. So after choosing a part $m$ with remaining sum $R$ (including $m$), the next part is a $\{2,3\}$-integer multiple of $m$, larger than $m$, that divides $R-m$.

The part $1$ is the first part, and the remaining parts sum to $45$ and form a chain whose first part $n_2$ divides $45$: $n_2\in\{3,9\}$.
- $n_2=9$: remaining sum $36$; next part a multiple of $9$, $>9$, dividing $36$: $18$ or $36$. $18$ leaves $18$, which cannot be written with parts $>18$. $36$ gives $(1,9,36)$.
- $n_2=3$: remaining sum $42$; next part a multiple of $3$, $>3$, dividing $42$: only $6$. Then sum $36$: next part a multiple of $6$, $>6$, dividing $36$: $12$, $18$ or $36$. $36$ gives $(1,3,6,36)$; $18$ leaves $18$, impossible; $12$ leaves $24$, next part a multiple of $12$, $>12$, dividing $24$: $24$, giving $(1,3,6,12,24)$.

So there are exactly three.

arml-2025-power-06b.title: Peel off one part at a time
arml-2025-power-06b.body:
Use the key fact: each part divides the sum of all parts from it onward. The first part $n_1$ divides $45$, so $n_1\in\{1,3,9\}$.
- $n_1=9$: as in (a), $(9,36)$.
- $n_1=3$: $(3,6,12,24)$ and $(3,6,36)$ (the enumeration of $3$ followed by chains summing to $42$ is the same as in (a)).
- $n_1=1$: the remaining sum is $44=4\cdot11$, so $n_2\in\{2,4\}$.
  - $n_2=2$: remaining sum $42$, next part a multiple of $2$, $>2$, dividing $42$: $6$. Remaining sum $36$: next part $12,18$ or $36$ as before, giving $(1,2,6,36)$ and $(1,2,6,12,24)$ ($18$ is impossible).
  - $n_2=4$: remaining sum $40$, next part a multiple of $4$, $>4$, dividing $40$: $8$. Remaining sum $32$: next part a multiple of $8$, $>8$, dividing $32$: $16$ or $32$. $32$ gives $(1,4,8,32)$; $16$ leaves $16$, impossible.

That makes six representations.

arml-2025-power-06c.title: A bijection
arml-2025-power-06c.body:
Representations of $n$ split into those with a $1$ ($p_1(n)$ of them) and those without. It suffices to show that the number without a $1$ is $p_1(n+1)$.

If $(n_1,\dots,n_r)$ is strictly chained of $n$ without a $1$, then $(1,n_1,\dots,n_r)$ is a strictly-chained representation of $n+1$ containing a $1$ ($1<n_1$ and $1\mid n_1$). Conversely, a strictly-chained representation of $n+1$ containing a $1$ has $1$ as its first part, and deleting it leaves a strictly-chained representation of $n$ without a $1$ (the remaining parts are still increasing and each divides the next). These maps are inverse to each other. Hence $p(n)=p_1(n)+p_1(n+1)$. ∎

arml-2025-power-07a.title: Bijection with representations of $n-1$
arml-2025-power-07a.body:
Parts that are $\{2,3\}$-integers not divisible by $3$ are exactly the powers of $2$. For a representation, call the sum of its power-of-$2$ parts its *binary part* $B$; since the parts are distinct, they are exactly the binary digits of $B$.

Let $\mathcal S$ be the set of representations of $n$ with at least one power-of-$2$ part ($B\ge1$), and $\mathcal T$ the set of representations of $n-1$.

*Map $\mathcal S\to\mathcal T$.* Keep the parts that are multiples of $3$; replace the power-of-$2$ parts (the binary digits of $B\ge1$) by the binary digits of $B-1$ (no parts if $B=1$). The new parts are $\{2,3\}$-integers, powers of $2$ are different from multiples of $3$, and powers of $2$ among themselves are distinct, so after sorting we get a double-base representation of $n-1$.

*Map $\mathcal T\to\mathcal S$.* Keep the multiples of $3$ and replace the power-of-$2$ parts, with sum $B'\ge0$, by the binary digits of $B'+1\ge1$; the result is a representation of $n$ with at least one power-of-$2$ part.

The two maps are mutually inverse ($B\mapsto B-1\mapsto B$), so $|\mathcal S|=|\mathcal T|=f(n-1)$. ∎

arml-2025-power-07b.title: Every representation qualifies
arml-2025-power-07b.body: If all parts of a representation of $n$ were multiples of $3$, then $3\mid n$. So when $3\nmid n$, every one of the $f(n)$ representations has a part that is not a multiple of $3$, and by the given fact there are exactly $f(n-1)$ of those. Hence $f(n)=f(n-1)$. ∎

arml-2025-power-07c.title: Divide by 3
arml-2025-power-07c.body:
By the given fact, $f(n-1)$ representations of $n$ have a part not divisible by $3$. It remains to show that the number of representations of $n$ in which all parts are multiples of $3$ is $f(n/3)$.

If $m$ is a $\{2,3\}$-integer divisible by $3$ then $m/3$ is a $\{2,3\}$-integer, and if $m$ is any $\{2,3\}$-integer then $3m$ is a $\{2,3\}$-integer divisible by $3$. So $(n_1,\dots,n_r)\mapsto(n_1/3,\dots,n_r/3)$ maps representations of $n$ with all parts multiples of $3$ to representations of $n/3$ (the order and the sum scale correctly), and $(m_1,\dots,m_r)\mapsto(3m_1,\dots,3m_r)$ is its inverse. Hence $f(n)=f(n-1)+f(n/3)$. ∎

arml-2025-power-08.title: Necessity, then a bijection
arml-2025-power-08.body:
Take $n=z+k$, so $\frac{n-z}k=1$ and $p(1)=1$.

**$k$ not a $\{2,3\}$-integer.** A multiple of $k$ that is a $\{2,3\}$-integer would force $k$ (a divisor of it) to be a $\{2,3\}$-integer, so no part can be a multiple of $k$; the only possible part is $z$, used at most once, so no representation of $n=z+k>z$ exists: count $0\ne1$.

**$k$ a $\{2,3\}$-integer, $z>0$, $z\nmid k$.** The parts are $z$ (at most once) and multiples of $k$. Since $0<z<k$, $z$ is not a multiple of $k$, so $z$ must be a part, and the other parts are multiples of $k$ summing to $k$: the only possibility is $(z,k)$. This is not strictly chained as $z\nmid k$, so the count is $0\ne1$.

**Sufficiency.** Let $k$ be a $\{2,3\}$-integer, with $z=0$ or $z\mid k$, $z<k$. Let $n>0$ with $n-z=km$ ($m\ge0$). Let $\mathcal S$ be the strictly-chained representations of $n$ with every part equal to $z$ or a multiple of $k$, and $\mathcal T$ the strictly-chained representations of $m$. Note: if $k\mid m'$ and both are $\{2,3\}$-integers then $m'/k$ is a $\{2,3\}$-integer, and $km'$ is a $\{2,3\}$-integer for any $\{2,3\}$-integer $m'$.

*Case $z=0$.* All parts are multiples of $k$ (no part can be $0$). Dividing every part by $k$ turns a member of $\mathcal S$ into a strictly-chained representation of $n/k=m$ (order, divisibility and sum are preserved), and multiplying by $k$ is the inverse.

*Case $0<z\mid k$, $z<k$.* Now $n\equiv z\not\equiv0\pmod k$, so some part is not a multiple of $k$, hence equals $z$; $z<k$ means it is the smallest part, $n_1=z$, and all other parts are multiples of $k$. If $n=z$ then $\mathcal S=\{(z)\}$ and $\mathcal T=\{()\}$. Otherwise map $(z,n_2,\dots,n_r)\mapsto(n_2/k,\dots,n_r/k)\in\mathcal T$; the inverse is $(m_1,\dots,m_s)\mapsto(z,km_1,\dots,km_s)$, which is strictly chained because $z\mid k\mid km_1$ and $z<k\le km_1$.

In both cases $|\mathcal S|=|\mathcal T|=p(m)$. ∎

arml-2025-power-09a.title: Inclusion-exclusion
arml-2025-power-09a.body:
Let $N=6n+1$. The first part $n_1$ divides every part, hence $N$; $N$ is coprime to $6$, so $n_1=1$, and $r\ge2$. The second part $n_2>1$ is a $\{2,3\}$-integer, so it is even or a multiple of $3$, and every later part is a multiple of $n_2$.

Let $A$ be the set of strictly-chained representations of $N$ with $n_2$ even, $B$ those with $3\mid n_2$, $C=A\cap B$ those with $6\mid n_2$. Then $p(N)=|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|C|$.

For $k\in\{2,3,6\}$ the representations with $k\mid n_2$ are exactly the strictly-chained representations of $N$ whose parts are $1$ or multiples of $k$ (the part $1$ is forced since $k\nmid N$). By the Fact with $z=1$ ($1\mid k$, $1<k$) their number is $p\!\left(\frac{N-1}k\right)$. So $|A|=p(3n)$, $|B|=p(2n)$, $|C|=p(n)$, and $p(6n+1)=p(3n)+p(2n)-p(n)$. ∎

arml-2025-power-09b.title: Split by the first part
arml-2025-power-09b.body:
If $3\mid n_1$ then every part is a multiple of $3$; by the Fact ($k=3$, $z=0$) there are $p(n/3)$ such representations. It remains to show that the number with $3\nmid n_1$ is $p(n-1)$. Let $\mathcal S$ be this set and $\mathcal T$ the set of strictly-chained representations of $n-1$.

In a member of $\mathcal S$, the parts not divisible by $3$ are powers of $2$; by the chain condition they come first: $n_1<\dots<n_j$ (each a power of $2$), followed by multiples of $3$, $n_{j+1}<\dots<n_r$. Let $B=n_1+\dots+n_j$ be the binary part, with binary digits exactly $n_1,\dots,n_j$ and top digit $n_j$; $B=n-(n_{j+1}+\dots+n_r)$ is a positive multiple of $3$, so $B\ge3$.

*Map $\mathcal S\to\mathcal T$.* Replace $n_1,\dots,n_j$ by the binary digits $x_1<\dots<x_m$ of $B-1\ge2$. Since $B-1<B$, the top digit satisfies $x_m\le n_j$; both are powers of $2$, so $x_m\mid n_j\mid n_{j+1}$ and $x_m<n_{j+1}$. The digits $x_i$ form a chain of powers of $2$. So $(x_1,\dots,x_m,n_{j+1},\dots,n_r)$ is a strictly-chained representation of $n-1$.

*Inverse.* Take a strictly-chained representation of $n-1$; its power-of-$2$ parts $y_1<\dots<y_k$ (a possibly empty initial segment) have sum $B'$, and the other parts are multiples of $3$ with sum $s$; $B'=n-1-s\equiv-1\pmod3$, so $B'\ge2$, $k\ge1$. Replace the $y_i$ by the binary digits of $B'+1$, where $B'+1=n-s\equiv0\pmod 3$ is not a power of $2$, so adding $1$ does not create a new top digit: the top digit of $B'+1$ equals $y_k$, which divides the next part. The result is a strictly-chained representation of $n$ whose first part is a power of $2$, i.e. in $\mathcal S$. The two maps are inverse to each other ($B\mapsto B-1\mapsto B$). So $|\mathcal S|=p(n-1)$ and $p(n)=p(n-1)+p(n/3)$. ∎

arml-2025-power-09c.title: Parts are $1$ or even
arml-2025-power-09c.body:
Let $(n_1,\dots,n_r)$ be strictly chained of $n\equiv2\pmod3$.

*No part is a power of $3$ other than $1$.* Suppose $n_i=3^a$ with $a\ge1$. Parts before $n_i$ divide $3^a$, so are powers of $3$, and at most $n_1$ can equal $1$ (the parts are distinct); parts from $n_i$ on are multiples of $3^a$. So every part except possibly $n_1=1$ is divisible by $3$, and $n\equiv0$ or $1\pmod3$, a contradiction.

Hence every part is $1$ or even (a $\{2,3\}$-integer that is odd is a power of $3$), and $1$ can only be $n_1$. So every strictly-chained representation of $n$ has all parts equal to $1$ or even.
- If $n$ is even there is no part $1$ (the sum would be odd), so all parts are even; by the Fact ($k=2$, $z=0$) there are $p(n/2)$ of them.
- If $n$ is odd, then the part $1$ must be present, and the Fact ($k=2$, $z=1$) gives $p\!\left(\frac{n-1}2\right)$.

In both cases $p(n)=p(\lfloor n/2\rfloor)$. ∎

arml-2025-power-09d.title: Two cases
arml-2025-power-09d.body:
**$n$ even, $n=2k$ ($k\ge1$).** Then $3n+1=6k+1$ and $3\lfloor\frac{n+1}2\rfloor-1=3k-1$. By (a) and (b) (with $m=3k$: $p(3k)=p(3k-1)+p(k)$),
$$p(6k+1)=p(3k)+p(2k)-p(k)=p(3k-1)+p(k)+p(2k)-p(k)=p(2k)+p(3k-1),$$
which is the claim.

**$n$ odd, $n=2k+1$ ($k\ge0$).** Then $N=3n+1=6k+4$ and $3\lfloor\frac{n+1}2\rfloor-1=3(k+1)-1=3k+2$, so we must show $p(6k+4)=p(2k+1)+p(3k+2)$. Since $3\nmid N$ the first part $n_1$ of any representation is a power of $2$. Split into representations containing $1$ and those not.

*Containing $1$* ($n_1=1$). The second part $n_2$ cannot be even (then all later parts are even and the sum $1+$even would be odd, but $N$ is even), so $n_2$ is a power of $3$, and all parts after $1$ are multiples of $3$. Conversely every representation whose parts are $1$ or multiples of $3$ contains $1$ (as $3\nmid N$). By the Fact ($k=3$, $z=1$) there are $p\!\left(\frac{N-1}3\right)=p(2k+1)$ of them.

*Not containing $1$.* Then $n_1\ge2$ is a power of $2$, so every part is even. Conversely an all-even representation has no part $1$. By the Fact ($k=2$, $z=0$) there are $p(N/2)=p(3k+2)$ of them.

Thus $p(6k+4)=p(2k+1)+p(3k+2)$. ∎
